newsitem.title: GERMANY: Christopher, Kohl agree on European security.
newsitem.headline: Christopher, Kohl agree on European security.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl agreed on Friday on future steps on European security in the post-Cold War era and Russia's place in that framework, U.S. officials said.

They decided a NATO foreign ministers' meeting scheduled for December "should not be a decision-making meeting but set the stage for next steps in the process" of NATO enlargement, one senior official said.
NATO leaders are expected to meet early in 1997 to decide which countries will be NATO's first new post-Cold War members.
Germany is at the forefront of those saying the move should be accompanied by some kind of formal charter or treaty defining NATO's relationship to Russia.

Kohl and Christopher met for 80 minutes in Bonn. The U.S. secretary then flew to Stuttgart where he was to deliver a policy speech on the broad approach the United States intended to take toward European security.

The meeting came on the eve of Kohl's hastily-arranged trip to see President Boris Yeltsin in Russia on Saturday, a visit which has taken on added significance with the news that Yeltsin is to undergo a heart operation this month.
Kohl and Christopher discussed Yeltsin's fragile health.
But they did not talk about how any change in leadership in Moscow could affect crucial NATO decision-making over the next year, U.S. officials told reporters en route to Stuttgart.

One official said that during Yeltsin's convalescence, Washington would continue to work with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, whose views were similar to Yeltsin's. "We can only work with one Russian government at a time," he said.
U.S. officials said Christopher agreed with Kohl's plans to "make sure Yeltsin understands the West's approach to European security".
This included reaffirming long-held U.S. views that Russia could not be allowed to veto NATO enlargement plans or delay the alliance's goal of taking in new members.
Countries widely viewed as topping the list are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Kohl will also stress during his visit that NATO wants to have "the closest relationship with Russia", U.S. officials said.
The alliance in 1995 offered a dialogue to Russia on their post-Cold War security ties, but only recently has Moscow resumed an intense discussion with the West on this topic.
Christopher previewed for Kohl the speech he will make in Stuttgart and in particular the U.S. broad approach to how the European security structure would evolve.
U.S. officials provided no details of the address, however.
Christopher was to give the speech on the 50th anniversary of an address in the same city by then secretary of state James Byrnes on reconstructing Europe after World War Two.

Byrnes made clear then the United States would remain engaged in Europe. He said Washington wanted to see vanquished Germany unified and reintegrated into Europe and able to help the continent's economic revival.
"This is a time of similar importance as it was in 1946," Christopher told reporters travelling with him from Washington.
"Then we had won the war but not won the peace. Now we are in a situation where we have prevailed in the Cold War but we've not fully made the adjustment and adaptation to the peace."
He said he intend to use his speech "to try to discuss overall European security issues...as (NATO) adapation... enlargement...and the NATO/Russia relationship."
Christopher arrived in Germany from Britain and France, where talks were dominated by the recent crisis in Iraq.
U.S. officials said Iraq figured only briefly in the Kohl-Christopher discussions, and said the secretary thanked the German chancellor for supporting the U.S. action.
